title: Lecture 14. Diagnostic and preventive measures for deviant adolescents
summary:
Tasks of diagnosing deviant adolescents Public discussion about «difficult» adolescents Overcoming assessment subjectivity Transition from a repressive to a supportive prevention strategy Example of a comprehensive assessment methodology Risk and protective (resilience) factors

1. Tasks of diagnosing deviant adolescents Let's imagine a situation where an adolescent comes to a school psychologist with some pronounced problems related to their personal characteristics or a difficult life situation, and who requires substantial professional help and long-term psychological and social support. In such cases, it could involve systematic violence at home or school, suicidal behavior, an antisocial or criminal lifestyle, drug use, etc. This situation differs significantly from one where a student's problem is resolved in one or several psychologist consultations.

In such a case, a comprehensive assessment of the child is required, which includes diagnosing their personality, social environment, and all aspects of their life situation. Such an assessment is needed, on the one hand, to determine the degree of risk to life and health, and on the other hand, to justify the directions of professional help required for such a child.

And although during regular individual counseling, a school psychologist can also operate with all the information listed above. But in complex cases, it's no longer enough to simply keep it in mind or in a notebook. It is necessary to:

collect information so that it is sufficiently complete and accurate. Moreover, a wide range of individuals may possess the necessary information: parents, teachers, friends, social workers, doctors, police officers, etc.; systematize information so that it characterizes all spheres of the adolescent's life, preferably with a quantitative assessment of risks in these spheres; store information in a formalized way, convenient for completion, transfer, and understanding by other specialists; be able to form a substantiated plan for individual preventive work; be able to evaluate the final effectiveness of this work. It can be said that the work of commissions for juvenile affairs and other organizations involved in individual preventive work, psychological-pedagogical, and social support for «difficult» adolescents is built upon the principles listed above. However, it cannot be said that such organizations fully adhere to these principles:

records filled out for adolescents who come to the attention of the Commission for Juvenile Affairs and Protection of Their Rights (KDNIZP) are often kept not in a formalized, but in a simple text format; the assessment of adolescent risks is largely subjective by specialists; consequently, individual preventive work plans do not always appear substantiated, nor are their results always achieved; information on adolescent cases is maintained and stored in a format that does not allow for statistical processing, which means the loss of valuable scientific and practical data.

To overcome the problems mentioned above, secondary screening or comprehensive assessment methodologies are used; in the domestic tradition, they are sometimes called socio-psychological tests. Such diagnostic methods are addressed to adolescents – representatives of a particular risk group who, as a rule, have already come to the attention of the police, judicial authorities, or commissions for juvenile affairs due to some behavioral problems, and help choose a more objective, optimal, and fair measure of restraint, punishment, or subsequent social support.

2. Public discussion about «difficult» adolescents Diagnostic methods for «difficult» adolescents developed primarily within the framework of juvenile justice — an area of law regulating the activities of the judicial system specializing in adolescent offenders. The emergence and development of juvenile justice itself resulted from a major public discussion that unfolded globally in the 19th century. It was believed that adolescent offenders differ from adult criminals. One cannot expect the same level of legal and civic consciousness development from adolescents as from adults. Adolescents' brains are not capable of regulating emotional impulses as effectively as adults'. And risky behavior, characteristic of adolescents, including illegal actions, is biologically predetermined by adolescence itself and serves as an important adaptive mechanism in the process of youth socialization.

It was believed that a fair and effective social policy in the field of justice and youth crime prevention should take into account scientific knowledge about adolescence and be based on reliable research data regarding factors of adolescent delinquency. This idea became the focus of public and professional attention in the 19th century with the emergence in several countries of a separate non-criminal court tasked with responding to juvenile offenses and emphasizing crime prevention rather than punishment. The main goal of the offense prevention system became supporting pro-social behavior among youth, their involvement in a system of healthy social relations, and, as a result, reducing criminal risks.

Such an approach to juvenile justice requires broader institutional coverage than justice itself and the imposition of sanctions for offenses. A complex system of interconnected measures implemented by various social institutions and organizations is needed, aimed at:

providing assistance to youth in developing social skills, in forming a sense of community with societal goals, and attachment to pro-social peers and adults; encouraging youth to take responsibility for admitted or proven offenses, as well as fulfilling obligations established by the court; ensuring the constructive participation of the adolescent's family members in court proceedings and their social environment in the prevention and rehabilitation process.

Moreover, such work should be based on prevention and social support methods proven effective, adapted to the specific life conditions of the adolescent offender and the capabilities of their environment. This requires the use of developed diagnostic and analytical tools and formalized approaches to assessing criminal risk in young people, as well as identifying individual resources for overcoming them.

3. Overcoming assessment subjectivity The first generation of such methodologies aimed to describe the widest possible range of indicators, approaching a clinical-anamnestic description. These methodologies were based on a set of judgments that doctors used in their daily practice to describe delinquent adolescents. When making assessments or predicting relapses of deviant behavior, doctors relied primarily on their own intuition. The assessments were expressed in an unstructured clinical conclusion.

However, individual judgments about different aspects of an adolescent's life did not allow for judging the overall level of risk in their behavior. Therefore, further improvement of assessment tools seemed necessary and logically justified, resulting in the emergence of second-generation methodologies. These were based on the statistical relationship between risk assessment obtained through the given instrument and the probability of re-offending. Such methodologies were developed based on empirical data, where model elements (factorial variables) are selected and statistically weighted in relation to the main criterion (resulting variable), for example, violence. The main task of these methodologies was to determine the level of risk and select appropriate sanctions or supervisory measures

This approach, called actuarial because it was borrowed from insurance practice, consists of an assessment based on a narrow range of easily recorded and statistically validated indicators, such as family income, education level, etc. The actuarial approach involves using a scoring system for various aspects of an adolescent's behavior and life situation related to committing an offense, and then weighting and summing the resulting scores into an overall risk behavior assessment. This procedure allows classifying a minor into one of several risk levels, for example: low risk, moderate risk, or high risk.

4. Transition from a repressive to a supportive prevention strategy By now, third-generation methodologies have gained widespread use, taking into account not only static but also dynamic factors, such as peer relationship problems or academic performance issues at school, etc. Thus, it became possible to monitor changes in adolescent behavior over the long term by comparing assessments obtained at different times.

The main achievement of third-generation methodologies was the emphasis not only on assessing risk factors but also on evaluating the adolescent's protective factors that contribute to their psychological well-being and social adaptation (see more details in «Factors of Health and Illness»). Differentiating the concept of risk from the concept of needs* when assessing an adolescent reflects the basic concept of the modern juvenile justice system, which aims to make decisions regarding adolescents based on a therapeutic rather than a repressive work strategy.

Needs – literally means «потребности, нужды» (needs, wants) in Russian. It is implied that this refers to the presence of protective factors in an adolescent, provided that their needs are met, and preventive programs should provide the adolescent with opportunities for this. Therefore, in Russian-language literature, instead of the word «потребности» (needs), the semantically closer word «возможности» (opportunities) has become established and is used here. Assessing an adolescent's behavioral risk is also an assessment of risk to public safety. Assessing needs (opportunities) determines the adolescent's existing potential to overcome behavioral disorders through therapeutic rather than repressive means. The correlation of these two assessments allows the court to answer the question: what can be an alternative to detention or imprisonment? The accuracy and precision of risk and needs assessments are the foundation of public trust in the juvenile justice system and an indicator of its effectiveness. From a therapeutic perspective, the accuracy of the assessments obtained from using a diagnostic methodology determines the precision in choosing types of assistance for the adolescent, which should be aimed at overcoming precisely those causes that led the adolescent to conflict with the law and cause obvious harm to their health.

Third-generation risk and needs assessment methodologies are standardized tools that help collect and synthesize information about an adolescent to assess risks for a specific adolescent and identify other factors that may reduce the likelihood of re-offending.

5. Example of a comprehensive assessment methodology An example of such a methodology is the «Assessing Risk and Need in Youthful Offenders» (RNA). Initially, it was designed to support the work of courts dealing with juvenile cases. For making informed decisions, imposing adequate punishment, and most importantly, preventive and supportive measures, courts require comprehensive yet concise information about the adolescent. Therefore, in 2008, the methodology was adapted for use in Russia. The Russian-language version of the methodology was named «Method of Structured Assessment of Risks of Repeated Offenses and Rehabilitation Opportunities for Minors» or, in short, «Risk and Needs Assessment (RNA)». In 2010, by decision of the Governmental Commission for Juvenile Affairs and Protection of Their Rights (No. 4, item 2.3.), the executive authorities of the constituent entities of the Russian Federation were recommended to use the methodology as a means of ensuring interagency cooperation between courts and prevention entities. In 2012, the methodology was adapted for use by educational institutions in one of the municipal districts of St. Petersburg (see details in Gurvich I.N., Antonova N.A., Dubrovsky R. G. Diagnosis and Prognosis of Deviant Behavior in Adolescents in the Educational Environment: A Teaching Manual. M.: RBF NAN, 2012. 144 p.).

Such a comprehensive assessment is usually conducted by a specialist who fills out the corresponding form (response sheet) for a specific observed adolescent. The methodology requires collecting a larger volume of individual data, which may include psychological testing, clinical interviewing, obtaining records from other institutions, and consulting with other experts observing the adolescent. Thus, the assessment procedure is used only for a limited group of adolescents, previously identified during primary screening or determined by other means as problematic. It is typically applied to adolescents with pronounced deviant and delinquent behavior and serves to form an individual therapeutic pathway, which is often considered an alternative to criminal punishment.

The methodology measures eight blocks of questions reflecting the behavioral, psychological, and socio-demographic characteristics of minors:

  • past and present offenses/court decisions;
  • family circumstances/parental functioning;
  • education/employment;
  • peer relationships;
  • substance abuse;
  • free time/leisure;
  • personality traits/behavior;
  • attitudes/social orientations.

The result of using the risk and needs assessment methodology is a protocol that links risk factors of various behavioral aspects and measures of necessary preventive intervention. This protocol provides grounds for deciding on the choice of specific measures concerning the adolescent, their sequence, and duration of application.

Comprehensive assessment methodologies have significant organizational advantages compared to clinical assessment or psychological tests:

saving time and effort for specialists assessing the adolescent, due to the formalization and scaling of assessment criteria, understood uniformly by different specialists involved in the assessment. That is, instead of a detailed textual description, almost the entire assessment procedure can be reduced to checking boxes and entering numerical values when filling out form fields; the ability to obtain a quantitative assessment of the risk level of committing a (repeated) offense across individual aspects of an adolescent's life and behavior, as well as an overall integrated risk assessment for a specific adolescent, which can serve as a substantiated and objective justification for individual preventive work; the ability to standardize the diagnostic methodology on specific groups of minors and obtain a standardized quantitative assessment of the risk level for any adolescent.

However, the discussed methodology has two significant drawbacks:

Its indicators do not fully meet the prevention tasks characteristic of the education system, Risk assessment norms were calculated long ago and for a sample of delinquent Canadian adolescents. Consequently, they are not applicable for use in our conditions.

Therefore, there is a need to create a proprietary secondary screening methodology that meets the current challenges of the Russian education system and is standardized on a sample of Russian students.

6. Risk and protective (resilience) factors The state of health or any deviant behavior is determined, on the one hand, by factors that increase the risk of the problem's occurrence, negative course, or outcome, and on the other hand, by factors that act in reverse: they reduce the likelihood of the problem's occurrence, alleviate the course of a condition, or contribute to problem resolution. The former are called risk factors, and the latter are called protective factors.

For example, a risk factor is that young people who have witnessed violent crimes or experienced abuse/neglect in their homes at a young age have an increased likelihood of engaging in violent acts later in life. Protective factors, on the other hand, can include an adolescent having friends or interests in their studies. Both types of factors are considered when planning preventive work.

While the presence and impact of risk factors can increase the likelihood of negative consequences for an adolescent, protective factors can reduce the occurrence of negative consequences and increase the adolescent's resilience (resistance) to adverse circumstances. For example, living in a disadvantaged and poorly maintained area is a risk factor for committing offenses, whereas supportive relationships with parents and other family members are a protective factor for an adolescent, which can have both direct and indirect effects.

It is precisely protective factors that serve as the main resources for prevention, on which specialists rely when planning an individual social support pathway for an adolescent. Therefore, protective factors require as thorough a study as risk factors.

Risk factors that we encounter in specialized literature are not merely products of someone's imagination but the result of research where the connection between that factor and the problem has been confirmed. That is, these are factors whose significance has been proven in various studies using statistical assessment methods. It is important to note that under different conditions or for representatives of other social groups, a different set of factors may be significant.

Below, as an example, is a summary of risk factors and protective factors for predicting the development of criminal (delinquent) behavior in adolescents. These factors have shown their significance in numerous studies on this topic and are systematized here by spheres of an adolescent's life.

Factors of Adolescent Criminalization

Risk Factors Protective Factors
Individual
1) Antisocial behavior and alienation (delinquent beliefs, general involvement in offenses):
  • ⚡ experience of police detention,
  • ⚡ vandalism,
  • ⚡ involvement in criminal groups and subcultures,
  • ⚡ rebelliousness,
  • ⚡ antisocial personality traits.*
2) Favorable attitude towards drug use, early onset of substance use:
  • positive attitude towards alcohol or drug use,
  • regular alcohol or drug use,
  • onset of drug use before age 15.
3) Early onset of aggression, violence, or other types of problematic behavior:
  • manifestation of aggression in an educational institution,
  • ⚡ arrests for violent crimes of any severity,
  • dropping out of school before graduating.
4) Violent victimization and children subjected to violence:
  • ⚡ sustained bodily injuries in a fight,
  • ⚡ threatened others or were injured by any weapon,
  • ⚡ witnessed violence,
  • ⚡ have experienced physical or sexual abuse.
5) Cognitive and neurological impairments, mental/behavioral health disorders:
  • academic underachievement,
  • emotional disorders,
  • brain injuries, past illnesses affecting the brain,
  • ADHD,
  • low self-control, impulsivity,
  • low IQ,
  • inability to organize daily life and plan for the future.·
1) Positive personal qualities:
  • stable personality,
  • pro-social orientation,
  • easy temperament,
  • purposefulness and positive future outlook,
  • socially outgoing,
  • low irritability and impulsivity.
2) Social competencies and problem-solving skills:
  • self-efficacy,
  • self-esteem,
  • engagement,
  • conflict resolution skills,
  • life skills,
  • resistance skills to unwanted interactions,
  • communication skills,
  • high IQ.
3) High social aspirations:
  • involvement in community life,
  • involvement in educational institution life,
  • planning for higher education and professional development,
  • having hobbies,
  • participation in purposeful activities (e.g., tutoring or volunteering),
  • positive cultural self-identity,
  • academic and other achievements.
Family
6) Family history of problematic behavior:
  • parents are intoxicated by alcohol or other substances,
  • parents receiving treatment for drug addiction,
  • alcohol consumption by pregnant mother,
  • children born with fetal alcohol syndrome,
  • ⚡ parents with criminal records or experience of police detention and imprisonment.
7) Family environment, parenting style:
  • children living outside the family,
  • lack of parental involvement in the child's life,
  • lack of adult care and support,
  • large family with many children,
  • extended family with child living with parents and grandparents,
  • highly anxious parents, hypercontrol and overprotection,
  • single-parent family,
  • parental death.
8) Victimization and child abuse:
  • registered cases of child abuse,
  • neglect,
  • non-payment of alimony,
  • requests for social services intervention,
  • divorce,
  • domestic violence, including emotional and verbal abuse.
9) Antisocial behavior of siblings:
  • ⚡ police detentions of siblings,
  • ⚡ older siblings encourage antisocial behavior.
10) Nature of punishment:
  • inconsistent discipline demands, ambiguity and contradiction in rules of conduct and household chores,
  • harsh discipline,
  • absence or lack of discipline and household rules,
  • poor supervision, lack of adult reaction to child's misbehavior,
  • low parental involvement in the child's educational life.
4) Effective positive parenting and stable family presence:
  • parental care,
  • family love and support,
  • clear rules and appropriate consequences,
  • child supervision,
  • fair and consistent disciplinary practices,
  • parental presence (at key moments: before and after school, dinner, bedtime, shared activities),
  • warm emotional ties with parents/family,
  • family cohesion,
  • good parental relationships with child's friends,
  • family support for the child's pro-social activities.
Peer-related
11) Association with delinquent or aggressive peers:
  • ⚡ involvement in criminal groups,
  • alcohol and drug use among peers,
  • peers' positive attitude towards alcohol or drug abuse,
  • violent friends,
  • rejection of the adolescent by pro-social peers,
  • ⚡ antisocial romantic partner.
5) Good peer relationships:
  • support from friends,
  • peers/friends with a positive outlook, healthy peer relationships,
  • conflict resolution skills,
  • ability to make and maintain relationships.
6) Positive peer role models:
  • group has established norms,
  • participation in community activities,
  • parental approval of friends,
  • extracurricular activities in educational institution,
  • healthy leisure,
  • adherence to generally accepted values and beliefs,
  • peers with good grades,
  • peers inclined towards pro-social behavior,
  • peers not involved in risky behavior,
  • peers who have close relationships with parents.
Education-related
12) Negative attitude towards educational institution, low motivation for learning:
  • poor academic performance/underachievement,
  • suspension or expulsion from an educational institution,
  • frequent changes of educational institution,
  • lack of motivation and academic goals,
  • low parental expectations regarding the child's further education,
  • low commitment to the educational institution,
  • disciplinary problems in elementary school.
13) Unsuitable climate in the educational institution:
  • verbal or physical violence, bullying, harassment by other students,
  • crime in the educational institution,
  • teacher burnout,
  • material and physical condition of the educational institution,
  • high level of distrust between teachers and students,
  • expulsion from the educational institution,
  • truancy, frequent absences from classes.
7) High expectations and above-average academic performance:
  • high GPA,
  • scholarships available,
  • good attendance,
  • student expectations from teachers,
  • behavior and responsibility.
8) Standards and rules of conduct in the educational institution:
  • presence of a formulated educational institution policy regarding safety, violence, and drugs,
  • student adherence to internal regulations,
  • presence of reward mechanisms for pro-social and high-achieving students,
  • strong friendly ties within the group,
  • participation in class/group activities and the community organization as a whole,
  • developed extracurricular activities and involvement in them.
9) Positive attitude towards the educational institution:
  • sense of connection with the educational institution,
  • attachment to teachers,
  • caring/supportive adults,
  • safe and caring environment,
  • use of proactive classroom/group management,
  • low staff turnover,
  • parental support for the educational institution,
  • high teacher morale.
Territorial, Community-related
14) Availability of alcohol and drugs:
  • non-compliance with regulations on alcohol sales to minors,
  • presence of accessible drug sales locations.
15) Community crime / high-crime area:
  • ⚡ level of violent crimes,
  • ⚡ homicide rate,
  • ⚡ level of adult drug-related crime,
  • ⚡ level of adult property crime.
16) Economic deprivation and poverty:
  • presence of disadvantaged neighborhoods with cheap housing,
  • families living below the poverty line,
  • living in a family without documents, medical insurance,
  • high unemployment rate in the area,
  • lack of social and professional prospects.
17) Social and physical disorganization:
  • feeling of insecurity in the area,
  • poor housing conditions,
  • vandalism, graffiti, broken streetlights in public places.

10) Disadvantaged but safe neighborhood, supportive environment:
  • public safety,
  • crime rate in the local community,
  • cohesion of local residents: sense of history and shared territory,
  • adolescent's connection to the community,
  • opportunities for community interaction: low-threshold youth clubs, local events,
  • positive social norms and values,
  • opportunities for youth community service and volunteering.

11) High expectations for youth:
  • community indicators of educational institution graduates,
  • scholarships from the local community,
  • public awareness campaigns.
  • graduate incentive programs.

12) Presence and involvement of caring and supportive adults:
  • presence of caring supportive adults and community neighbors,
  • positive relationships with adults outside the family (neighbors, mentors, coaches, etc.)*
💡
Note: Here and further,⚡ highlighted in color specific factors of the problem are those related only to it. Other factors — non-specific, meaning they can be predictors of any other stress outcomes. As we can see, compared to non-specific factors, there are relatively few specific ones. This emphasizes that the core of preventing negative phenomena in the adolescent environment is non-specific, meaning it should be aimed at reducing the overall stress level among adolescents, rather than solving specific problems.
